summary: The note describes a Midwestern revival of heritage grains and legumes led by farmers, chefs, bakers and educators who want to reclaim regional flavors, biodiversity and sustainability. It profiles people such as Martin Henderson, Jillian MacArthur and Ethan Taylor, and covers terroir, education programs, farming challenges and growing market demand. The outlook is hopeful, though it is too early to say whether heritage varieties will replace modern ones.
one_line: Midwestern farmers, chefs and educators are reviving heritage grains and legumes, restoring regional flavor and biodiversity while facing farming challenges and building market demand.
key_facts: Martin Henderson is a fourth-generation farmer in Ohio whose fields hold amaranth, einkorn, emmer and spelt; the author visited on September 15, 2023.
Martin Henderson and his wife Clara began returning to heritage grains in the spring of 2024 and initially faced skepticism from neighboring farmers.
Jillian MacArthur, a botanist turned farmer, started a small-scale operation in Wisconsin on November 2, 2023, and grows lentils among other crops.
Through much of the 20th century agriculture shifted to crops bred for yield and ease of mechanical harvesting, which reduced diversity.
By the early 2020s, soil degradation, loss of wildlife habitat and a yearning for past flavors sparked interest in ancient crops.
Ethan Taylor, a Minneapolis chef, discovered heritage grains in the winter of 2024 and now collaborates with farmers like Martin and Jillian; he praises farro risotto.
Lynda Foster runs a small bakery in Illinois and sources her grains exclusively from heritage grain farmers, wanting to taste the season's sunshine and rain in the grains.
The Midwestern Heritage Grain Alliance is a farmer collective that holds workshops and seed swaps and partners with local schools.
Tomás Rivera, a middle school teacher, has been involved in a farm-to-school program since October 2024.
Heritage crops often need different planting and harvesting methods and have unique vulnerabilities to local pests and diseases.
Farmers draw on both historical texts and innovative farming technology to adapt old practices; Martin says 'We're learning as we go.'
Co-ops, farmers' markets and some supermarkets now carry heritage grain products such as stone-ground flours and artisanal breads.
Clara Henderson says 'People crave authenticity in their food. They want to taste something real.'
The note says it is too early to tell whether heritage grains and legumes will completely replace modern counterparts.
